name: Hivites
summary: A Canaanite people found from Shechem to the foot of Mount Hermon. They are best known through the Gibeonites, who tricked Joshua into a treaty with worn-out sandals and mouldy bread and then served at Israel's altar for generations.
name_meaning: Uncertain; possibly 'villagers' or 'tent-dwellers' (from Hebrew hawwah, a tent-village). Some scholars equate them with the Hurrians.

origin.account: The Hivite is listed among Canaan's descendants. Genesis places them at Shechem in Jacob's day, Joshua at Gibeon, and Joshua and Judges in the north 'under Hermon in the land of Mizpeh' and in Mount Lebanon.

lineage.notes: Esau's wife Aholibamah was a granddaughter of 'Zibeon the Hivite'. Genesis 36 calls the same Zibeon a Horite, one reason some scholars link the two groups.

homeland.region: Scattered: Shechem, the Gibeon tetrapolis, and the Lebanon–Hermon region
homeland.description: The Gibeonite league had four cities north-west of Jerusalem: Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth and Kirjath-jearim. Northern Hivites lived in the valleys of Lebanon, from Mount Baal-hermon to the entering in of Hamath.
homeland.modern_location: Central West Bank (Shechem, Gibeon) and southern Lebanon / Mount Hermon.

places.name: Gibeon
places.note: 'A great city, as one of the royal cities'; famous pool.

places.name: Kirjath-jearim
places.note: Gibeonite city where the Ark rested twenty years.

places.name: Shechem
places.note: Ruled by Hamor the Hivite in Jacob's time.

timeline.event: Shechem son of Hamor the Hivite violates Dinah; Simeon and Levi deceive and massacre the city.
The Gibeonites trick Israel into a treaty. When discovered, they are made 'hewers of wood and drawers of water' for the house of God.
Joshua rescues Gibeon from five Amorite kings; this is the battle where the sun stands still.
Hivites in Lebanon are left 'to prove Israel'.
Saul had broken the oath to the Gibeonites by killing them; in David's day a three-year famine follows until seven of Saul's descendants are handed over. Rizpah's vigil follows.
Remaining Hivites put to forced labour.
Men of Gibeon return from exile and help rebuild Jerusalem's wall.

religion.practices: The Gibeonites were bound to serve at 'the altar of the LORD' in the place He would choose. Gibeon later held the great high place where Solomon asked God for wisdom.

importance: The Gibeonite story shows how seriously Scripture treats an oath made in God's name. Israel's leaders were deceived because they 'asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD', yet they had to keep the treaty. When Saul broke it generations later, the whole land suffered famine. The Gibeonites — Canaanites who chose to submit rather than fight — ended up serving at God's altar and helping rebuild Jerusalem.

impact.how: The Shechem affair stained Simeon and Levi, and Jacob cursed their anger on his deathbed.
Learned the cost of not seeking the LORD's counsel.
Seven descendants died to answer Saul's bloodguilt.
Guarded her sons' bodies from harvest to rain, moving David to bury Saul's house.

key_verses.text: And the men took of their victuals, and asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD. And Joshua made peace with them, and made a league with them, to let them live: and the princes of the congregation sware unto them.
And Joshua made them that day hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation, and for the altar of the LORD, even unto this day, in the place which he should choose.

Then there was a famine in the days of David three years, year after year; and David enquired of the LORD. And the LORD answered, It is for Saul, and for his bloody house, because he slew the Gibeonites.

fate.summary: Absorbed into Israel. The Gibeonites lived on as temple servants and as citizens of Judah after the exile. Jewish tradition identifies them with the Nethinim, the temple servants of Ezra's time.

today.summary: No Hivite people exist today. Gibeon is the village of al-Jib north of Jerusalem, where the great rock-cut pool of Gibeon can still be seen.
today.modern_legacy: The phrase 'hewers of wood and drawers of water' comes from the Gibeonite story.

archaeology.name: Pool of Gibeon and jar-handle inscriptions
archaeology.discovered: 1956–1962 excavations by James B. Pritchard at el-Jib
archaeology.location: Site: el-Jib; finds: University of Pennsylvania Museum
archaeology.significance: A rock-cut shaft with a spiral staircase, and dozens of jar handles inscribed 'gb'n' (Gibeon), confirming the site's identity.
